Investors have piled into Palantir stock as the company has shown itself to be an early winner in the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution. Palantir offers its customers a way to easily and quickly harness the power of AI, and that's translated into tremendous demand and revenue growth.
The AI story continues, with key players such as chip designers and cloud service providers speaking of high demand, and that paints a bright future for Palantir. Could $20,000 invested in this tech company help you retire a millionaire? Let's find out.
Image source: Getty Images.
We'll start by considering the Palantir story so far. This company isn't new to the scene; it's actually been around for more than 20 years, and in its early days, mainly served government customers. Palantir develops software systems that gather a customer's data and put it to use. And a key moment took place a few years ago when Palantir released its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP), a system that leverages the power of AI to analyze and use the data to make truly game-changing decisions.
Governments, particularly the U.S. government, have continued to appreciate Palantir's strengths, and this has kept government revenue climbing in the double digits. But the new element for Palantir has been the growth it's seen in its commercial business. The commercial customer has rushed to get in on AIP, and this has supercharged revenue growth in recent years.
The latest quarter is the perfect example. U.S. commercial revenue advanced 149% to $764 million, while U.S. government revenue climbed 90% to $809 million. And total contract value (TCV) is on the rise too -- the company closed TCV of $3.3 billion, up 49% from the same period last year. U.S. commercial customer count has also skyrocketed from less than 20 just a few years ago to more than 600.

Now, let's return to our question: As it's firing on all cylinders, can this AI player help you retire a millionaire?
We'll start by considering how a $20,000 investment in Palantir a few years ago would have played out. If you had invested that sum in the company a decade ago, today the value of your investment would be more than $390,000. That, along with investment in a variety of other quality stocks across industries, could have helped you along the path to millions.
Moving forward, Palantir could have room to run, particularly over the long term. Today, it trades for 116x forward earnings estimates, which isn't cheap, but it's important to keep in mind that the stock traded for more than 250x about a year ago. So investors will pay a premium for Palantir stock, suggesting that it could move higher from today's level.
It's also important to note that AI is just starting to be applied in the real world, so significant growth here may lie ahead. And Palantir's U.S. commercial customer count shows us two points that are very positive: Customer count is growing quickly, so momentum is there. But customer count still is low enough to offer considerable room for growth. All of this sets the stage for significant commercial revenue growth in the quarters and years to come.
Palantir, on its own, is unlikely to make you a millionaire. It's rare when one stock alone, even a top performer, will do the entire job, and it's too risky to bet on just one or two stocks to build wealth. But as part of a portfolio of quality stocks, this AI player could help you reach that goal as you retire.

A 93% Growth Quarter Restarted Palantir’s Rally
Shares rose 2.36% over the past week and are up 6.53% year to date at $189.36 this morning. The stock is 8.8% below its $207.52 52-week high and 78% above its $106.37 low.

The adjusted operating margin reached 62%, and Palantir guides for $4.50 billion to $4.70 billion in adjusted free cash flow for the year. 21 analysts rate the stock a buy or strong buy. Under the most optimistic scenario, shares reach $219.27.
Valuation and Dilution Could Cap the Upside
Shares trade at 159x trailing earnings and 85x forward earnings. Stock-based compensation was $265 million in Q2, and gains on Palantir’s SpaceX stake added $0.03 to GAAP EPS. Government contracts terminable for convenience pose a risk.
Two analysts rate the stock a sell or strong sell, and the downside scenario points to $170.18. Q2 free cash flow of $1.220 billion far exceeded stock-based compensation, while adjusted expenses rose 37% due to AI platform investment and technical hiring.

Snowflake (NYSE:SNOW) competes for enterprise AI data budgets with 35.09% revenue growth but a GAAP operating loss of $263 million.
MongoDB (NASDAQ:MDB) sells AI-ready databases with 30.5% revenue growth.
Palantir is growing close to three times as fast as either peer and at far higher margins. Against that group, the 24/7 Wall St. price target looks reasonable, and arguably conservative.
Palantir’s Growth Tips the Scale Toward Our Buy Rating
The 24/7 Wall St. price target of $202.08 carries a buy rating and 90% confidence. What tips the scale is Palantir’s ability to keep speeding up growth while margins expand.
I would view shares more favorably if U.S. commercial growth holds above 100% into 2027. I would grow more cautious if the pace of deal closings slows while the stock still trades at 85x forward earnings.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) Stock: Partners With Armada on Sovereign AI Infrastructure
Palantir and Armada combine software and modular data centers for customer-owned sovereign AI deployments.
By Yasmin WernerOctober 2, 2026No Comments3 Mins Read
Palantir partners with Armada to expand sovereign AI infrastructure deployments.
Armada is named Palantir’s inaugural Certified Modular Data Center Partner.
Joint infrastructure keeps models, data, and hardware under customer control.
Modular data centers support faster deployment across secure operating sites.
Armada’s Sovereign AI Grid links distributed sites for stronger system resilience.
Palantir Technologies partnered with Armada to deliver sovereign artificial intelligence infrastructure for governments and enterprises. Palantir Technologies (PLTR) traded at $189.93, down 0.06%, after retreating from an intraday peak near $194.50. The companies will combine Palantir software with modular data centers manufactured in the United States and allied nations.
Palantir Names Armada Modular Data Center Partner
Palantir named Armada its inaugural Certified Modular Data Center Partner under the new agreement. The partnership combines Palantir’s Sovereign AI Operating System with Armada’s modular infrastructure and distributed network. Together, the companies aim to give customers direct ownership over computing systems, models, and stored data.
The offering targets organizations seeking infrastructure that operates within their own security boundaries. Therefore, customers can deploy open-weight models without depending on computing resources controlled by outside cloud providers. Armada also supports deployments at locations where existing power capacity can support new computing infrastructure.
Palantir will validate its operating system on Armada’s Galleon modular data centers. Its software stack includes AIP, Ontology, Foundry, and Apollo across the joint infrastructure. Meanwhile, Armada will provide the hardware, management software, and connectivity required across distributed deployments.
Partnership Extends Palantir Sovereign AI Architecture
The agreement expands Palantir’s existing Sovereign AI Operating System reference architecture developed with NVIDIA. That framework supports computing infrastructure that customers physically own and directly operate. The Armada partnership now brings that structure into modular data centers designed for faster deployment.
Customers can run open models and adapt them using proprietary company or government data. They can also serve those models through Palantir platforms without moving information outside controlled infrastructure. As a result, organizations can maintain direct authority over computing hardware and model operations.
Armada manufactures the modular data centers in the United States and selected allied nations. The companies designed the system for traditional sites, remote locations, and environments without standard network connections. The modular approach also reduces dependence on lengthy construction schedules for conventional data centers.
Armada Infrastructure Supports Distributed AI Deployments
Armada’s software platform manages open-source models for model tuning and inference across customer-owned infrastructure. The platform can function without Armada’s cloud services and supports fully air-gapped systems when required. It also monitors computing equipment, power systems, and cooling conditions across each deployment.
The Sovereign AI Grid connects individual locations into a broader distributed computing system. Organizations can spread important workloads across several sites instead of depending on one facility. This structure provides additional operational resilience when individual locations face outages or infrastructure problems.
Demand for locally controlled computing infrastructure has increased as organizations review cloud dependence and supply-chain exposure. Governments also seek stronger control over sensitive data, computing resources, and model deployment locations. Palantir and Armada now plan to address those requirements through an integrated customer-owned infrastructure stack.

Is Palantir’s Cash Flow Keeping Ahead of Share Dilution?
Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR) is producing substantially more cash as its revenue expands. The investment question is whether that growth is large enough, per share, to compensate for stock compensation and the price investors are paying. A rising company-wide cash balance can coexist with a demanding shareholder valuation.
At September 30, Palantir's market capitalization was approximately $449.49 billion. The stock traded at roughly 134 times trailing free cash flow. Strong business execution is therefore necessary but may still be insufficient if much of its benefit is already capitalized in the share price.
Is Palantir's Cash Flow Keeping Ahead of Share Dilution?
Fast-growing enterprise software carries very different prices. Our Palantir-versus-Snowflake analysis asks whether Palantir or Snowflake better justifies its valuation, with ownership costs helping determine the answer.
Cash flow and compensation measure different things
First-half operating cash flow was $2.115 billion and capital expenditure $21.96 million, producing about $2.093 billion of simple free cash flow. First-half stock-based compensation was $466.8 million. Subtracting that compensation produces an illustrative $1.627 billion owner-cost proxy, roughly 22% below reported free cash flow.
This adjusted figure is neither GAAP free cash flow nor the exact amount required to offset dilution through repurchases. Stock awards are expensed according to accounting rules, while actual share issuance and the cash price of buybacks occur differently. The subtraction is useful as a sensitivity because compensation transfers part of the business's value to employees, even when it does not immediately consume cash.
The share count rose approximately 1.79% over the preceding year at the market-data snapshot. That is less dramatic than the growth in revenue, supporting the bullish argument that existing owners are still benefiting. It also means a company-wide growth rate should not be presented as an identical per-share growth rate.

Broadcom's custom AI chips are just getting started
Nvidia might dominate the conversation when it comes to GPUs, but Broadcom is becoming an increasingly important player in AI infrastructure.

As the software market shifts toward products driven by artificial intelligence (AI), investors comparing enterprise software names may find themselves choosing between Salesforce (CRM -0.84%) and Palantir Technologies (PLTR -0.68%). This comparison looks at which company offers the better balance of value and growth.
Salesforce describes itself as a global leader in customer relationship management (CRM) technology and is now focused on Agentforce, its line of autonomous AI agents. Palantir sells software platforms that governments and companies use to integrate their data and apply AI to daily operations. For investors researching AI stocks to buy, the two companies present very different financial profiles.
Salesforce sells cloud-based software that helps businesses manage customer relationships and sales pipelines. Its annual report for fiscal 2026, which ended on Jan. 31, 2026, lists 83,334 employees and states that the company sells to businesses across almost every industry. On Aug. 26, 2026, Salesforce said annual recurring revenue from Agentforce had passed $1.5 billion. It completed its acquisition of Fin, an AI customer agent company formerly known as Intercom, on Sept. 10, 2026.
In fiscal 2026, revenue reached approximately $41.5 billion, up 9.6% from the prior fiscal year. Net income was nearly $7.5 billion, and net margin rose to 18% from 16.4%. About $1.0 billion in net gains from strategic investments contributed to that improvement, compared with a small net loss on those investments a year earlier.
As of Jan. 31, 2026, Salesforce had about $14.4 billion in total debt and $59.1 billion in shareholder equity, a debt-to-equity ratio of about 0.2x. Its current ratio, which compares current assets with liabilities due within a year, was roughly 0.8x.
The debt picture has changed since then. Salesforce issued about $25 billion in debt in the quarter that ended April 30, 2026, to fund an accelerated share repurchase, and its July 31, 2026, balance sheet shows $39.3 billion in debt against $38.4 billion in equity, a ratio of about 1.0x.
Free cash flow, defined as operating cash flow minus capital expenditures, was about $14.4 billion in fiscal 2026. Stock-based compensation (SBC) equaled roughly 23.4% of operating cash flow, which is worth noting because SBC is a non-cash expense that is added back in the cash flow statement.
Palantir develops software platforms that help organizations integrate their data and operations, and it sells them to government agencies and commercial customers.
Government customers supplied 54% of its 2025 revenue. Palantir also works with other companies that investors follow as tech stocks, including a collaboration with Nvidia (NVDA +1.34%) announced on Sept. 10, 2026, and a global partnership with Fujitsu (FJTSF +0.97%). Its commercial customer count reached 870 for the 12 months ended June 30, 2026, up 26% from a year earlier.
In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, revenue reached roughly $4.5 billion, a 56.2% year-over-year increase. Palantir reported net income of about $1.6 billion. Net margin was about 36.3%, up from 16.1% in 2024.
Palantir had no debt outstanding as of Dec. 31, 2025, resulting in a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.0x. Its current ratio at that date was approximately 7.1x, indicating ample liquid assets to cover short-term liabilities. Free cash flow, calculated the same way as for Salesforce (operating cash flow minus capital expenditures), was about $2.1 billion.
Palantir's own adjusted free cash flow, which adds back employer payroll taxes tied to stock-based compensation, was about $2.3 billion. SBC equaled roughly 32% of operating cash flow.
Salesforce competes with established enterprise software vendors and AI-native start-ups in a market that its annual report calls highly competitive. Salesforce and its Slack unit sued Microsoft (MSFT +0.92%) in London's High Court in April 2026, alleging that the tying and bundling of Teams harmed competition.
Microsoft has said the case lacks merit, and the outcome is uncertain. Salesforce must also integrate large acquisitions such as Informatica, which closed in fiscal 2026, and Fin, and it now carries far more debt than it did at the start of the fiscal year. On Sept. 29, 2026, it also agreed to acquire Listen Labs, an AI customer research company, in a deal it expects to close in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027.
Palantir's annual report flags a limited number of customers that account for a substantial portion of its revenue, with the top three supplying 16% of 2025 revenue, and a sales cycle it calls long and unpredictable.
The company depends on third-party computing infrastructure. It also warns that news coverage or other outside scrutiny of the company or its leadership could harm its reputation. A shareholder lawsuit that a federal court dismissed in April 2025 was still on appeal as of June 30, 2026.
Salesforce trades at a much lower forward P/E, which compares the stock price to future earnings estimates, and a much lower P/S ratio, which measures price relative to sales over the past 12 months.
Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.
Which stock would I buy in 2026?
Salesforce looks like the better buy to me, with the caveat that it's a slower-growing and more indebted company than the fiscal 2026 figures above suggest. On Aug. 26, 2026, management guided for revenue growth of 11% to 12% in fiscal 2027, which ends in January 2027.
By its own math, more than a quarter of that growth comes from the Informatica acquisition. Salesforce also borrowed heavily earlier this year to fund its accelerated share repurchase. Its debt has more than doubled since January and roughly equaled shareholder equity at the end of July. The appeal is the price.
A business that turns about a third of its revenue into free cash flow, at a forward P/E in the mid-teens, leaves room for Agentforce to grow slowly without the investment case falling apart.
Palantir is growing far faster. Its revenue nearly doubled in the second quarter, and on Aug. 3, 2026, management raised its full-year outlook. The catch is a forward P/E ratio more than five times Salesforce's, which leaves the stock with little cushion if growth cools.
Growth rates this high are also hard to sustain as a company gets bigger. I'd rather hold Palantir as a small position in a diversified portfolio than pay that premium for a large one. Even so, a company expanding this quickly with no debt has earned a spot on a growth investor's watch list.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) Stock: Partners With Armada on Sovereign AI Infrastructure
Palantir and Armada combine software and modular data centers for customer-owned sovereign AI deployments.
By Yasmin WernerOctober 2, 2026No Comments3 Mins Read
Palantir partners with Armada to expand sovereign AI infrastructure deployments.
Armada is named Palantir’s inaugural Certified Modular Data Center Partner.
Joint infrastructure keeps models, data, and hardware under customer control.
Modular data centers support faster deployment across secure operating sites.
Armada’s Sovereign AI Grid links distributed sites for stronger system resilience.
Palantir Technologies partnered with Armada to deliver sovereign artificial intelligence infrastructure for governments and enterprises. Palantir Technologies (PLTR) traded at $189.93, down 0.06%, after retreating from an intraday peak near $194.50. The companies will combine Palantir software with modular data centers manufactured in the United States and allied nations.
Palantir Names Armada Modular Data Center Partner
Palantir named Armada its inaugural Certified Modular Data Center Partner under the new agreement. The partnership combines Palantir’s Sovereign AI Operating System with Armada’s modular infrastructure and distributed network. Together, the companies aim to give customers direct ownership over computing systems, models, and stored data.
The offering targets organizations seeking infrastructure that operates within their own security boundaries. Therefore, customers can deploy open-weight models without depending on computing resources controlled by outside cloud providers. Armada also supports deployments at locations where existing power capacity can support new computing infrastructure.
Palantir will validate its operating system on Armada’s Galleon modular data centers. Its software stack includes AIP, Ontology, Foundry, and Apollo across the joint infrastructure. Meanwhile, Armada will provide the hardware, management software, and connectivity required across distributed deployments.
Partnership Extends Palantir Sovereign AI Architecture
The agreement expands Palantir’s existing Sovereign AI Operating System reference architecture developed with NVIDIA. That framework supports computing infrastructure that customers physically own and directly operate. The Armada partnership now brings that structure into modular data centers designed for faster deployment.
Customers can run open models and adapt them using proprietary company or government data. They can also serve those models through Palantir platforms without moving information outside controlled infrastructure. As a result, organizations can maintain direct authority over computing hardware and model operations.
Armada manufactures the modular data centers in the United States and selected allied nations. The companies designed the system for traditional sites, remote locations, and environments without standard network connections. The modular approach also reduces dependence on lengthy construction schedules for conventional data centers.
Armada Infrastructure Supports Distributed AI Deployments
Armada’s software platform manages open-source models for model tuning and inference across customer-owned infrastructure. The platform can function without Armada’s cloud services and supports fully air-gapped systems when required. It also monitors computing equipment, power systems, and cooling conditions across each deployment.
The Sovereign AI Grid connects individual locations into a broader distributed computing system. Organizations can spread important workloads across several sites instead of depending on one facility. This structure provides additional operational resilience when individual locations face outages or infrastructure problems.
Demand for locally controlled computing infrastructure has increased as organizations review cloud dependence and supply-chain exposure. Governments also seek stronger control over sensitive data, computing resources, and model deployment locations. Palantir and Armada now plan to address those requirements through an integrated customer-owned infrastructure stack.

Fast-growing enterprise software carries very different prices. Our Palantir-versus-Snowflake analysis asks whether Palantir or Snowflake better justifies its valuation, with ownership costs helping determine the answer.
Cash flow and compensation measure different things
First-half operating cash flow was $2.115 billion and capital expenditure $21.96 million, producing about $2.093 billion of simple free cash flow. First-half stock-based compensation was $466.8 million. Subtracting that compensation produces an illustrative $1.627 billion owner-cost proxy, roughly 22% below reported free cash flow.
This adjusted figure is neither GAAP free cash flow nor the exact amount required to offset dilution through repurchases. Stock awards are expensed according to accounting rules, while actual share issuance and the cash price of buybacks occur differently. The subtraction is useful as a sensitivity because compensation transfers part of the business's value to employees, even when it does not immediately consume cash.
The share count rose approximately 1.79% over the preceding year at the market-data snapshot. That is less dramatic than the growth in revenue, supporting the bullish argument that existing owners are still benefiting. It also means a company-wide growth rate should not be presented as an identical per-share growth rate.
Valuation raises the required performance
Short interest was 60,184,903 shares at the September 15 settlement, about 2.8% of float, with 2.24 days to cover. The valuation question remains about future cash per share, regardless of that dated positioning.
Annualizing the first-half free cash flow produces about $4.19 billion. At the current market capitalization, that illustrative pace implies around 107 times cash flow. Annualizing the owner-cost proxy gives $3.25 billion and a multiple near 138. The figures are not forecasts and do not replace a full-year model; they show how the compensation assumption changes valuation on the same period basis.
To bring the equity value down to 40 times sustainable annual free cash flow would require roughly $11.24 billion of annual cash generation. That is about 2.7 times the annualized first-half figure before any compensation adjustment. At 30 times, the required annual amount rises to nearly $15 billion. A high price requires a larger future business even when current margins are strong.

Palantir Technologies has become one of the biggest names in artificial intelligence (AI), but the current boom is creating opportunities well beyond software. Broadcom (AVGO +3.35%) is providing hardware that could rival Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs), while Applied Digital (APLD +5.05%) is building the physical infrastructure that hyperscalers need to run it all. So for investors who are looking for promising AI bets other than Palantir, these two stocks deserve a closer look.

Broadcom's custom AI chips are just getting started
Nvidia might dominate the conversation when it comes to GPUs, but Broadcom is becoming an increasingly important player in AI infrastructure.
Instead of competing head-on with Nvidia in general-purpose processors, Broadcom specializes in custom chips and networking technology that help some of the biggest companies build their own AI infrastructure. This puts it in a solid position with hyperscalers that are looking to develop chips specifically designed for their AI workloads.
The company is already working with major technology companies such as Alphabet, Meta Platforms, and OpenAI, positioning it at the center of the industry's growing demand for custom chips.
That demand is already translating into meaningful growth. The company's latest quarterly results showed AI semiconductor revenue more than tripling year over year, and management expects more acceleration in the current quarter.

The company also raised its longer-term AI revenue outlook, underscoring its confidence that hyperscalers' data center investments will continue to climb over the next several years.
But more importantly, Broadcom's opportunity extends beyond the chips themselves. Its networking technology is used to connect thousands of AI processors into huge computing clusters, giving the company exposure to multiple parts of the AI building boom.
Meanwhile, its established software business includes its VMware AI Factory, which makes it easier for customers to deploy and manage AI infrastructure, launch AI models faster, and improve cost efficiency through automation.
But chips are only part of the equation. As AI computing requirements continue to grow, the industry also needs to keep adding physical infrastructure. That's where Applied Digital comes into the picture.
Applied Digital is building the data centers powering AI
Applied Digital offers a different way to participate in the AI boom. Instead of designing chips or developing AI models, the company builds and runs the data centers that power AI workloads.
It has been expanding its portfolio of AI campuses, attracting major customers through long-term lease agreements that provide it with strong visibility into its future revenues. It has secured three deals with an investment-grade hyperscaler across different campuses, bringing its total contracted capacity to $36 billion.
Moreover, Applied Digital continues to make progress on its existing projects. Its Polaris Forge 1 campus in North Dakota has already kicked off operations, and additional capacity will keep coming online as construction continues. The company also secured further financing to expand its data center portfolio, helping turn its pipeline into operational facilities.

Another important development was its move to hive off its cloud services business into a new public company, ChronoScale (CHRN -0.83%). This will allow Applied Digital to focus more on developing and running large-scale AI campuses. That should help strengthen its business, especially as hyperscalers race to secure more computing capacity to train and run advanced AI models.
Although Broadcom and Applied Digital are in different parts of the AI supply chain, both stand to benefit from the huge investments being made in the technology.
Two different ways to invest beyond Palantir
For investors who want a steadier way to play the AI theme than Palantir offers, Broadcom's diversified chip and software business, along with its exposure to surging demand for custom AI chips and networking technology, makes it the safer of these two picks.
Applied Digital, on the other hand, is the higher-risk, higher-reward option, as it's betting big on building the data centers needed to power the next generation of AI.
Which one is the better choice for your portfolio likely depends on how much risk you're willing to take on.
